hello.note: Literally 'are you good?'; Wiktionary's own phrase entry glosses Wĩ mwega? as 'how are you', with the reply Ĩĩ, ndĩ mwega ('yes, I'm fine').

good_morning.note: Literally 'news of the morning'; rũciinĩ (morning) is dictionary-attested, but no source confirms this full greeting as a set phrase, so treat it as a lower-confidence build by analogy with Ũhoro waku.

good_evening.note: Literally 'news of the evening'; hwaĩ-inĩ (in the evening) is dictionary-attested, but this full greeting is likewise an unconfirmed, lower-confidence build.

goodbye.note: Said to those staying; lit. 'be left with goodness'. Listed as a set idiom under wega on Wiktionary and confirmed in a Wikipedia Gikuyu-language sample-phrase table.

how_are_you.note: Literally 'your news?'; attested in a Wikipedia Gikuyu-language sample-phrase table ('How are you: Ũhoro waku'); the reply is Nĩ wega.

thank_you.note: Wiktionary has this exact phrase glossed as 'thank you'. Thengiũ, from English, is an increasingly common variant (Njagi 2016).

youre_welcome.note: Literally 'it's not a thing'; ti (not) and ũndũ (thing/matter) are each dictionary-attested, but no source gives a fixed Kikuyu idiom for 'you're welcome'. Checked Wiktionary, Glosbe, and Tatoeba for a rival set phrase (e.g. a Swahili-style karibu loan) and found none for Kikuyu, so this transparent negation calque -- common across nearby Bantu languages for 'it's nothing' -- is kept as the plainest honest option, flagged lower-confidence rather than dropped.

no_problem.note: Same phrase as you're welcome; no distinct Kikuyu set phrase for 'no problem' turned up in any source checked either, so it shares the same lower-confidence flag rather than being invented separately.

please.note: Literally 'I beg/beseech you', built on the dictionary-attested verb gũthaitha ('to beseech', Armstrong 1940). No source gives a dedicated word for 'please' in Kikuyu, so this verb-based construction is a lower-confidence but plain, honest stand-in.

excuse_me.note: Literally 'I have regret'; kĩeha (grief, sorrow, regret) is dictionary-attested, but this specific apology formula is not confirmed as a set phrase, so treat it as a lower-confidence build.

sorry.note: Same phrase as excuse me; kĩeha is grief or regret, dictionary-attested, but this exact apology usage is likewise unconfirmed and lower-confidence.

yes.note: Wiktionary lists Ĩĩ as the Kikuyu interjection for 'yes', the antonym of Aca.

no.note: Wiktionary lists Aca as the Kikuyu negative particle for 'no', the antonym of Ĩĩ.

of_course.note: Literally 'it is true'; ma (truth/truly) is directly dictionary-attested (Benson 1964). Checked against Ĩĩ mũno ('yes, very much') as a rival, but no source confirms a fixed idiom for 'of course' either way, so this plain, transparent affirmation is kept as the more honest pick over a fancier unattested one.

amazing.note: Literally 'it's very good!'; wega (goodness) and mũno (very, much) are each dictionary-attested, but no source confirms this as a set exclamation for 'amazing', so it is a lower-confidence build.

delicious.note: Said of food; mwega is the adjective form of wega. Mirrors the amazing entry and is not confirmed as a food-specific idiom, so treat it as lower-confidence.

cheers.note: A short toast; literally 'good' or 'goodness' (dictionary-attested noun), but no source confirms toast usage in Kikuyu, so this is a lower-confidence extension.
